analysis.one_liner: Ends tax breaks for corporations that shift profits and headquarters offshore.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 77 cosponsors, all Democrats, but the House Ways and Means Committee never acted on it and it died when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would roll back several corporate tax breaks created or preserved by the 2017 tax law. It would tax offshore profits of U.S.-owned foreign subsidiaries each year at the normal corporate rate instead of a steeply discounted one, limit interest deductions for large multinational groups, tighten the rules on companies that renounce U.S. incorporation to lower their taxes, and treat foreign corporations managed from the United States as domestic for tax purposes. It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit if the revenue raised from closing these offshore breaks reduces deficits or funds public priorities. Domestic companies that keep their profits, jobs, and headquarters in the United States also gain, because the bill removes tax advantages their offshore-moving rivals enjoy. Working people gain indirectly where the tax advantage for moving jobs or booking profits abroad is removed.

how_it_helps.text: The bill taxes the tested income of foreign subsidiaries of U.S. companies each year as earned and repeals the reduced-rate deduction for foreign-derived intangible income and global intangible low-taxed income, so profits booked offshore are taxed at the full corporate rate [S2, S3].
It repeals the exclusion of foreign oil and gas extraction income from the income taxed on a controlled basis, closing a carve-out for that industry [S2, S3].
It limits interest deductions for members of large international financial reporting groups, reducing the incentive to load U.S. companies with debt to shrink their taxable income [S2, S3].

It tightens the rules for inverted corporations, treating a foreign-organized company as domestic when former U.S. owners hold 80 percent or more of it, or when management and control remain primarily in the United States with significant U.S. business activity [S2, S3].

It treats foreign corporations that are publicly traded or hold $50 million or more in assets and are managed and controlled primarily in the United States as domestic for income tax purposes [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Multinational corporations that shift profits to low-tax jurisdictions, companies that inverted their incorporation, hedge funds and investment firms managed from the United States but organized offshore, and oil and gas companies with foreign extraction income would all pay more tax. Higher compliance and planning costs for large multinationals would also be part of the cost.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises taxes on U.S.-based multinationals' foreign earnings without directing the revenue to any specific benefit for workers or families; the fiscal gain depends entirely on how Congress later uses the money [S2, S3].

Critics of taxing foreign earnings at the full U.S. rate argue it can expose companies to double taxation when host countries also tax the same income, which may put U.S.-headquartered firms at a competitive disadvantage against foreign rivals in overseas markets.

The management-and-control test for foreign corporations relies on Treasury regulations that the bill directs the Secretary to write, so its real-world reach over offshore-organized investment firms would depend on rules not yet in existence [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets real tax advantages for moving profits and headquarters offshore, and most of its provisions apply the same treatment the U.S. already applies to domestic income. The main honest trade-off is competitiveness: taxing foreign earnings at the full U.S. rate, with limited credits against high foreign taxes, can disadvantage U.S. firms operating abroad, and the bill offers no direct worker benefit, only revenue. On balance the closed loopholes and leveled playing field for domestic employers outweigh those costs, but the bill was written as a statement of principle rather than a negotiated package.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Ways and Means Committee, which never held a markup or vote on it, and it expired when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Lloyd Doggett introduced the bill on February 27, 2018 with 25 original cosponsors and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S3, S5].
It attracted 77 cosponsors, all of them Democrats [S4].
The Ways and Means Committee, which held the bill, took no further action: no hearing, no markup, no vote, and the bill was never reported to the House floor [S5].

The bill's targets were the new international provisions of the 2017 tax law, including the reduced tax rate on foreign intangible income and the deemed return on overseas investments, so its fate was effectively sealed once that law had passed with Republican majorities in both chambers [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational corporations and offshore-organized investment firms kept the tax breaks the bill would have repealed, and the Treasury forgoes the revenue those changes would have raised. The Ways and Means Committee's majority avoided a vote on the issue entirely.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Multinationals keeping their offshore tax breaks

for.name: Rep. Lloyd Doggett
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 25 original cosponsors

against.name: Rep. Kevin Brady
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill; never scheduled a hearing or markup, keeping it from any vote

sides.party_line_note: All 78 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the Republican-led committee buried the bill without action [S4, S5].

industries.industry: Multinational corporations that shift profits offshore
industries.note: The bill taxes their foreign subsidiaries' income each year at the full corporate rate and repeals the steep discounts created by the 2017 tax law, removing a major advantage of booking profits abroad [S2, S3]. Ordinary taxpayers bear the cost of those breaks when they are preserved.

industries.industry: Hedge funds and investment managers organized offshore but run from the U.S.
industries.note: Firms with $50 million or more in assets under management that are managed and controlled primarily in the United States would be taxed as domestic corporations, closing a common offshore structure for investment funds [S3].

The bill would treat foreign-organized successors to U.S. companies as domestic when ownership or management remains mainly in the United States, undoing the benefit of relocating headquarters on paper [S2, S3].

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies with foreign extraction income
industries.note: The bill repeals the exclusion of foreign oil and gas extraction income from the income taxed on a controlled basis, ending a specific carve-out for that industry [S2, S3].
